items.title: Fastfetch 2.72 System Information Tool Adds NVMe Drive Health Monitoring

items.title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
items.summary: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower. The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet, which broke apart in the 1850s. When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm. This means that there were way more meteors than usual.

items.title: Ant Group Releases LingSante-3.1-flash: An Open-Weight MoE Model with 560B Total Parameters and 25B Activations per Token
items.summary: Ant Group has open-sourced LingSante, a family of medical and health AI models behind health app Afu. The flagship, LingSante-3.1-flash, is an open-weight medical AI model with 560B total parameters and 25B active per token. It ships under the MIT license with a 1M-token context window. On the new InclusionMed evaluation, it scores highest among open models. It is a self-hostable model trained for clinical reasoning, medical search and tool-using agents. items.title: Frozen language model helps predict materials properties with roughly 95% less training time
items.summary: Discovering new materials often involves predicting their properties before investing time and resources in making and testing them in the laboratory. Machine-learning models are widely used to estimate important properties, such as band gap and formation energy, helping researchers narrow down candidate materials. More recently, large language models (LLMs) have offered a flexible way to represent materials through text for property prediction.

items.title: This week the highly anticipated London Museum opened
items.summary: This week on Dezeen, we revealed the transformation of London's 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum, completed by architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects. Ten years in the making, the renovated Victorian market building now contains two main gallery spaces – one an airy open space and the other a subterranean exhibition at Roman street level – displaying artefacts from London's history. Another major museum that opened this week is Kanal in Brussels, which at 40,000 square metres, claims to be "Europe's largest museum development".

items.title: Make the most of the new moon on Dec. 8 and get closer views of the stars with the Celestron Inspire 100AZ
items.summary: The new moon on Dec. 8 is the perfect time to stargaze at targets that might otherwise be shrouded by moonlight, allowing clearer views of stars, star clusters and some deep-sky objects. items.title: China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes
items.summary: Much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors, as U.S. export restrictions make it harder to buy advanced chips in the region. But making an AI server involves far more than securing its processors. The printed circuit boards (PCBs) connecting chips, memory, and networking equipment are becoming harder to manufacture, and Chinese companies are racing to supply the materials and equipment they require.

items.summary: COCHISE COUNTY, AZ (AZFamily) — SpaceX’s proposed $50 billion supercomputer campus in southeastern Arizona has a name: Colossus 3. items.summary: Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities was winding down Friday and power was slowly being restored to hundreds of thousands of customers as some high-tide flooding threats remained following a round of holiday storms. items.summary: Gen Z protests in India in July demanded the resignation of the Minister for Education following a string of student suicides. After millions engaged in peaceful protests throughout the country, the minister eventually resigned. items.title: Medieval Chain Mail Armour Discovered in 15th-Century Shipwreck
items.summary: Maritime archaeologists investigating the wreck of a Danish royal warship that sank in 1495 have uncovered well-preserved fragments of exceptionally high-quality medieval chain mail armour. The discovery could offer new insights into the military equipment carried aboard late medieval warships and the German mercenaries who served on them. An international research team from the University of Southampton, Södertörn University and Stockholm University made the discovery while investigating the Gribshunden, also known as Griffin, one of the most significant medieval shipwrecks in the Baltic Sea.

items.summary: One of the biggest reasons I see people give for not moving from Windows to Linux is that the latter has a reputation for being hard to set up. items.title: FCC authorizes SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million Starmind AI satellites by 2040
items.summary: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed as orbital data centers for artificial intelligence computing. The order, released by the FCC’s Space Bureau on November 25, marks the first U.S. authorization of its kind. It sets a 14-year window for SpaceX to place the full network in low Earth orbit. If fully built, Starmind would dwarf every satellite launched in the history of spaceflight. According to Jonathan McDowell’s catalog dated November 18, roughly 28,800 satellites have been placed in orbit since Sputnik in 1957.

items.summary: Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time. items.title: Verifiable Social Reasoning for LLM Assistants
items.summary: We introduce an evaluation framework based on multi-agent social simulations that quantifies how well AI assistants understand social situations from users' subjective narratives. In our framework, a target agent with a hidden motive interacts with other agents including one representing the user, who then consults the evaluated assistant to infer the target’s motive, providing verifiable ground truth by construction.

items.title: Tolleson Thanksgiving dinner brings community together for more than 40 years
items.summary: Hundreds of West Valley residents gathered for a Thanksgiving meal in Tolleson, continuing a community tradition that has brought families, students and volunteers together for more than four decades. The Tolleson Union High School District's annual Thanksgiving Day Community Dinner has become a holiday staple, offering residents a chance to enjoy a traditional meal while connecting with neighbors and celebrating the season. For Javier Garcia Ramos, the event is a family tradition that stretches back generations.

items.title: Sun news: Hello, AR4584!
items.summary: Sun news November 28: Hello, AR4584 Today’s top story: Meet AR4584! After three days of flaring from just behind the sun’s southeast limb, this region has now rotated into view and gotten its number. Now that the sun’s edge no longer hides it, its flares measure as being stronger, too. items.title: Beeswax and pine link crocodile mummies made centuries apart at one Egyptian site
items.summary: In a practice spanning centuries, ancient Egyptians mummified thousands of crocodiles they associated with Sobek, a god linked to the Nile, fertility and royal power. items.title: a review of midcentury kinetic environments: when artists turned entire rooms into moving machines
items.summary: when motion became a property of space Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, an international network of artists began to explore the possibilities of kinetic art at the scale of architecture. Motors and electrical circuits found their way into museum galleries, where entire interiors could be animated with moving structures and artificial light. In some cases, the machinery responded to the viewer’s presence. An early precedent for these experiments came from the Bauhaus. items.title: Section 232 solar tariffs take effect December 4: Here’s what the industry needs to know
items.summary: Beginning next Friday, Dec. 4, the U.S. solar industry enters a new trade regime as the Trump Administration’s Section 232 proclamation on polysilicon and downstream solar components takes effect. Signed on Aug. 6 following a Department of Commerce national security investigation, the action replaces expired safeguard duties with a supply-chain-wide framework designed to prevent foreign equipment from undercutting domestic manufacturing economics. items.title: GRIDSERVE secures £420m to refinance debt and expand charging network

items.summary: Greenhushing refers to the deliberate practice by companies of downplaying, concealing, or remaining silent about their environmental goals, climate commitments, and sustainability initiatives. items.title: EVs Outsold Gas And Diesel Cars Combined In The EU In October
items.summary: EVs outsold gas and diesel cars combined in the EU in October, reversing the result from a year earlier. Germany and France drove much of the growth, though the shift looks different elsewhere in the EU. Hybrids still lead the market, even as a wider choice of affordable EVs gives buyers more reasons to go fully electric. The European Union registered about 24,000 more new cars last month than in October 2025. items.title: Norse Atlantic ends flights: How Iran war continues to batter aviation
items.summary: The Norwegian airline Norse Atlantic has filed for bankruptcy for its main operating unit, cancelling all flights and halting ticket sales, as soaring jet fuel prices triggered by the United States-Israel war on Iran claim another operator. items.title: AI simulates electron hops over far longer times than conventional quantum calculations

Electrons can jump from one atom to another, changing the forces between atoms as well as the material's chemical reactivity.

items.title: Why An Airbus A321XLR Captain Crossing The Atlantic Thinks About Diversions Differently Than A Boeing 787 Captain
items.summary: When a Boeing 787 Dreamliner and an Airbus A321XLR cross the North Atlantic on the same day, the two aircraft may follow similar tracks and land at the same destination. items.title: Many languages, one common neural code
items.summary: Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message. Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way. Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study published today in Nature Neuroscience, the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages.

items.title: 6 Greatest Libraries of Antiquity and the Lost Knowledge They Guarded
items.summary: We often imagine knowledge in the ancient world as held in oral tradition and rare handwritten texts passed down within specific groups. And more than just actively collecting texts from far and wide, scholars came up with systems to catalog collections so that they could be explored and studied. Unfortunately, the six greatest libraries of the ancient world have all been lost to destruction and decay.

items.title: Why Science Cannot Agree on What Counts as Normal
items.summary: Normality seems to be embedded in our society through norms, expectations, and scientific tests, as well as criteria for pathological states. Yet, it is hard to define. We intuitively know what is normal (or at least believe we do), though this depends on our immediate cultural and natural environment and history. Normality is also a cornerstone of many scientific disciplines, but even there its definition remains contested. Is normality a statistical average, a reflection of biological self-regulation, or a socially constructed ideal?

items.summary: The leap from RKO Radio Pictures circa 1940 to Paul Schrader in the 1980s is like chasing store-brand vanilla ice cream with Cold Stone’s Cat in the Hat’s Cotton Candy Catastrophe. items.title: The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks

items.title: This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain
items.summary: A naturally derived dietary supplement called urolithin A may help the brain get more oxygen and nutrients when it needs them most. items.title: Why Oliver Reed Was One of Horror’s Greatest Scream Kings
items.summary: The arrival of Ken Russell ’s uncut version of The Devils (1971) in theaters this year has not only kindled interest in the films of the director but also in the work of the film’s star, Oliver Reed. items.title: Listen to the Music of the Ancient World: From 40,000-Year-Old Flutes to Ancient Greek Songs
items.summary: There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world. We can learn its languages, at least the ones that have left behind decipherable writings; we can behold its artifacts; we can visit its ruins. But nothing gets us quite as close to entering the consciousness of our distant forebears as hearing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In the new Archaeologist’s Notebook video above, Giselle Király gives us a tour through ancient musical history, explaining the instruments of those times that survive in one form or another today.
